name: OILS-3
description: Question bank for OILS-3: Oops, I Learnt Something! (3rd Sem Engineering Edition).

1.topic: What is Git, why version control, git init, the .git folder

mcq.q: What is Git's main advantage over manually copying files (like report_v2.docx, report_FINAL.docx)?
opts: A) Git automatically sends your files to your teammates
B) Git records a cryptographic timeline of snapshots so you always know what changed, when, and who changed it
C) Git compresses all your files into a zip archive
mcq.explain: Git's core value is its snapshot timeline — every commit is a dated, labelled snapshot of the entire project. You can compare any two points in history, see who changed what, and restore any state instantly.
mcq.wrong_a: Git doesn't automatically send files — you explicitly push commits to a remote like GitHub. That's a separate step.
mcq.wrong_c: Git doesn't compress your files into a zip. It stores efficient object snapshots inside the hidden .git folder.

mcq.q: Where does Git physically store the repository's entire history, configuration, and commits on your computer?
opts: A) In a hidden '.git' folder located at the root of your project directory
B) In the Windows Registry or macOS System Library
C) On an external cloud server that must always be online
mcq.explain: Git is fully decentralized. The entire repository history, commits, tags, and branches live inside the hidden '.git' folder right in your project root.
mcq.wrong_b: Git never stores project version history in the Windows Registry or macOS System Library. Everything is contained within the project's .git folder.
mcq.wrong_c: Git does NOT require a cloud connection to store history. Your local .git folder contains 100% of the repository data even completely offline.

mcq.q: What happens if you delete the hidden '.git' folder inside your project?
opts: A) Nothing — Git backs it up to GitHub automatically
B) Your project files stay but ALL Git history, branches, and commits are permanently lost
C) Git recreates it automatically on the next git status
mcq.explain: The .git folder IS the repository. Deleting it destroys all version history, branches, and commits. Your working files survive but Git tracking is gone completely.
mcq.wrong_a: Git does not automatically backup to GitHub. You must explicitly push. And even then, local history could differ.
mcq.wrong_c: Git never auto-recreates the .git folder. You'd have to run git init again, starting history from scratch.

mcq.q: Which command transforms a plain folder into a Git-tracked repository?
opts: A) git start
B) git create
C) git init
mcq.explain: git init initializes a new repository by creating the .git directory with all the metadata structures Git needs to start tracking changes.
mcq.wrong_a: There is no 'git start' command in Git. This is a common misconception.
mcq.wrong_b: There is no 'git create' command. That is not a valid Git subcommand.

mcq.q: Git is described as a 'distributed' version control system. What does distributed mean?
opts: A) Every developer has the full repository history on their own machine
B) Git distributes files across multiple hard drives for redundancy
C) Git requires at least 3 servers to function
mcq.explain: Distributed means every clone of a repository contains the COMPLETE history. You can commit, branch, and view history entirely offline. No central server is required to work.
mcq.wrong_b: Git does not distribute files across multiple drives. All history is in the single .git folder.
mcq.wrong_c: Git requires zero servers to operate locally. A remote server like GitHub is optional.

mcq.q: Before running 'git init', what should you ideally do first?
opts: A) Run 'git config --global user.name' and 'git config --global user.email' to identify yourself
B) Create a GitHub account and set up SSH keys
C) Install a GUI like GitHub Desktop
mcq.explain: Every Git commit records who made it. Setting your name and email via git config --global ensures every commit is properly attributed to you from the start.
mcq.wrong_b: GitHub and SSH keys are for remote operations. For local git init and commits, only your name and email config matter.
mcq.wrong_c: A GUI is entirely optional. Git is a command-line tool and works perfectly without any graphical interface.

cmd.scenario: You created a brand new folder called 'portfolio' for your website and opened your terminal inside it.
cmd.task: Run the command to initialize a new Git repository in the current folder:
cmd.hint: Use the command that initializes Git tracking: git <subcommand>
cmd.output: Initialized empty Git repository in /portfolio/.git/
cmd.why: git init creates the hidden .git metadata folder where Git records all commits, trees, and blobs.

cmd.scenario: Before writing code, you want to verify that the Git CLI is properly installed and check its version.

cmd.hint: Use the '--version' flag with the git command.
cmd.output: git version 2.44.0.windows.1
cmd.why: git --version confirms that Git is installed on your PATH and reports the active release.

cmd.scenario: You just ran git init. Now you want to set your name so all commits are attributed to you.
cmd.task: Set your global Git username to 'Ada Lovelace':
cmd.hint: Use 'git config --global user.name' followed by the name in quotes.
cmd.output: (No output — Git silently saves the config to ~/.gitconfig)
cmd.why: git config --global user.name sets your identity for every repository on this machine. Git embeds this in every commit you create.

cmd.scenario: You want to see ALL Git settings currently active on your machine (name, email, editor, etc.).
cmd.task: List all current Git configuration values:
cmd.hint: Use 'git config' with the '--list' flag.
cmd.output:
user.name=Ada Lovelace
user.email=ada@example.com
core.editor=vim
cmd.why: git config --list dumps every config key-value pair from system, global, and local scopes combined.

cmd.scenario: You initialized a repo but made a mistake and want to check what files Git is tracking right now.
cmd.task: Show the current state of the working directory and staging area:
cmd.hint: Use the command that reports which files are modified, staged, or untracked.
cmd.output:
On branch main
No commits yet
nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)
cmd.why: git status is your most-used command — it shows what's tracked, modified, staged, and what branch you're on.

2.topic: Three-stage workflow: Working Directory, Staging Area (git add), Commit History

mcq.q: You edited a file and want it in the next commit. What is the correct ORDER of steps?
opts: A) git commit → git add → git push
B) Edit file → git add to Staging Area → git commit to History
C) git push → git commit → git add
mcq.explain: Files flow: Working Directory (edit) → Staging Area (git add) → Commit History (git commit). You must stage before you can commit.
mcq.wrong_a: You can't commit before staging. git commit only packages files that are already in the Staging Area.
mcq.wrong_c: git push uploads commits to a remote — it comes AFTER committing, not before.

mcq.q: Why does Git have a Staging Area instead of committing changes directly from the working folder?
opts: A) Staging is a required technical limitation of file system permissions
B) It lets you craft clean, atomic commits by choosing exactly which files and lines belong together
C) The Staging Area automatically compresses files to save disk space
mcq.explain: The Staging Area (Index) is Git's superpower — it lets you selectively include exactly the right changes in each commit, keeping your history clean and meaningful.
mcq.wrong_a: The Staging Area is a deliberate design choice for precision, not a file system limitation.
mcq.wrong_c: The Staging Area has nothing to do with compression. Compression happens in Git's object database.

mcq.q: Which git command moves a file from the Working Directory into the Staging Area?
opts: A) git stage
B) git commit
C) git add
mcq.explain: git add moves changes from your Working Directory into the Staging Area (the Index), making them ready to be included in the next commit.
mcq.wrong_a: There is no 'git stage' command in standard Git.
mcq.wrong_b: git commit records what is already in the Staging Area — it doesn't move files there.

mcq.q: After running 'git add myfile.py', where does myfile.py now live in Git's three stages?
opts: A) It is permanently saved to Git history
B) It is in the Staging Area (Index), ready to be committed
C) It has been pushed to GitHub
mcq.explain: git add moves the file's current state into the Staging Area (Index). It's NOT yet committed. You still need git commit to permanently record the snapshot.
mcq.wrong_a: git add alone does NOT create a commit. The file is staged but not saved to history yet.
mcq.wrong_c: git add has nothing to do with GitHub. It only moves changes into the local Staging Area.

mcq.q: What does 'git status' report about a file you've edited but NOT yet staged?
opts: A) 'Changes to be committed'
B) 'Changes not staged for commit'
C) 'Untracked files'
mcq.explain: 'Changes not staged for commit' means Git knows the file exists and is tracking it, but you've made edits since the last commit that haven't been staged yet.
mcq.wrong_a: 'Changes to be committed' means the file IS already staged with git add.
mcq.wrong_c: 'Untracked files' means Git has never seen this file before — it was never added.

cmd.scenario: You edited two files: 'style.css' and 'server.py'. You only want to prepare 'server.py' for the next commit.
cmd.task: Stage ONLY the file 'server.py' into the staging area:
cmd.hint: Use 'git add' followed by the exact filename you want to stage.
cmd.output:
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged server.py" to unstage)
	modified:   server.py
cmd.why: git add <filename> stages a single file, keeping other modified files unstaged in your working directory.

cmd.scenario: You edited multiple files across different folders and want to stage ALL modified and untracked changes at once.
cmd.task: Stage ALL modified and new files in the current repository:
cmd.hint: Use 'git add' with a single dot '.' or '--all' to stage everything.
cmd.output: (All modified and new files in the current directory are staged into the Index ready for commit)
cmd.why: git add . stages all changes in the current directory and subdirectories into the staging index.

cmd.scenario: You accidentally staged the wrong file (config.env) and need to remove it from staging without deleting it.
cmd.task: Unstage 'config.env' (keep the file's changes in the working directory):
cmd.hint: Use 'git restore' with a flag that targets the staged version.
cmd.output:
Unstaged changes after reset:
M	config.env
cmd.why: git restore --staged removes the file from the Index but leaves your working copy unchanged — perfect for accidental git adds.

cmd.scenario: You want to see exactly WHAT changed inside a file before staging it — line by line differences.
cmd.task: Show the unstaged line-by-line diff of your working directory changes:
cmd.hint: Use the command that shows differences between your working files and the last commit.
cmd.output:
diff --git a/server.py b/server.py
--- a/server.py
+++ b/server.py
@@ -10,6 +10,7 @@
+    print('Hello World')
cmd.why: git diff shows the exact line-by-line changes in your working directory that have NOT yet been staged.

3.topic: Recording commits: git commit -m, commit messages, git log, git status

mcq.q: What does a Git commit actually store?
opts: A) Only the files that changed since the last commit (a diff/patch)
B) A complete snapshot of ALL tracked files at that exact moment in time
C) A compressed zip of the entire project folder
mcq.explain: Every Git commit stores a full snapshot of every tracked file, not just diffs. Git is efficient — identical file content is stored only once as a shared blob object.
mcq.wrong_a: Git stores full snapshots, not patches. Tools like 'git diff' compute patches on demand from two snapshots.
mcq.wrong_c: Git does not create zip files. It stores blob objects in its own efficient object store inside .git/objects.

mcq.q: Which of the following is a GOOD commit message?
opts: A) 'fix'
B) 'feat: add email validation to registration form'
C) 'asdfgh changed stuff'
mcq.explain: A good commit message uses a type prefix (feat/fix/docs/refactor) and describes WHAT changed and WHY in a concise imperative sentence.
mcq.wrong_a: 'fix' is too vague — a future developer (including you) cannot understand what was fixed without reading the diff.
mcq.wrong_c: A meaningless message makes git log useless. The message should tell a story of the project's evolution.

mcq.q: What command shows you the full history of commits in the current branch?
opts: A) git history
B) git show
C) git log
mcq.explain: git log shows the commit history with SHA hash, author, date, and message for each commit. Add --oneline for a compact view.
mcq.wrong_a: There is no 'git history' command in standard Git.
mcq.wrong_b: git show displays details about a SINGLE commit, not the full history.

mcq.q: What flag makes 'git log' display each commit on a single compact line?
opts: A) git log --compact
B) git log --short
C) git log --oneline
mcq.explain: git log --oneline shows the first 7 characters of the SHA hash and the commit subject on one line each — perfect for quick history scanning.
mcq.wrong_a: There is no --compact flag in git log.
mcq.wrong_b: There is no --short flag for git log (--short exists in git diff for a different purpose).

mcq.q: You committed with the wrong message. How do you fix the MOST RECENT commit's message (before pushing)?
opts: A) git commit --fix
B) git commit --amend -m "correct message"
C) git revert HEAD
mcq.explain: git commit --amend replaces the most recent commit with an updated version. It rewrites history, so use it only on commits not yet pushed to a shared remote.
mcq.wrong_a: There is no --fix flag in git commit.
mcq.wrong_c: git revert creates a NEW commit that undoes a previous one — it doesn't edit a commit message.

cmd.scenario: You staged your changes and are ready to save a permanent snapshot with the message 'feat: add user authentication'.
cmd.task: Create a commit with the message 'feat: add user authentication':
cmd.hint: Use 'git commit' with the '-m' flag followed by the message in quotes.
cmd.output:
[main 7f2b91c] feat: add user authentication
 2 files changed, 48 insertions(+)
cmd.why: git commit -m "message" permanently records all staged changes into a new commit snapshot.

cmd.scenario: You want to see the last 5 commits in your project history in a compact one-line format.
cmd.task: Show the last 5 commits in compact one-line format:
cmd.hint: Use 'git log' with '--oneline' and a number flag like '-5'.
cmd.output:
7f2b91c feat: add user authentication
3c1a44f fix: correct email regex
a99d001 docs: update README
2f8e993 refactor: extract auth helper
0b3c821 feat: initial project setup
cmd.why: git log --oneline -5 shows the 5 most recent commits in a readable compact format, great for a quick history scan.

cmd.scenario: You just committed but forgot to include one file. You want to add it to the SAME commit without creating a new one.
cmd.task: Stage the missed file 'config.py' and amend it into the last commit (keep the same message):
cmd.hint: Use 'git commit --amend' with '--no-edit' to keep the existing message.
cmd.output:
[main 9a2b81d] feat: add user authentication
 3 files changed, 52 insertions(+)
cmd.why: git commit --amend --no-edit rewrites the last commit to include newly staged files without changing the message.

cmd.scenario: You want to see the full details (author, date, diff) of the very last commit.
cmd.task: Show the complete details of the most recent commit:
cmd.hint: Use the command that shows a single commit's full info and diff.
cmd.output:
commit 7f2b91c...
Author: Prajwal <p@example.com>
Date:   Mon Nov 10 2026

    feat: add user authentication

diff --git a/auth.py...
cmd.why: git show (or git show HEAD) displays the commit metadata plus the full diff of changes introduced by that commit.

4.topic: Branching: git branch, git checkout, git switch, HEAD pointer

mcq.q: What is a Git branch technically?
opts: A) A full copy of the repository stored in a separate folder
B) A lightweight movable pointer to a specific commit
C) A compressed backup of all project files
mcq.explain: A branch is just a lightweight pointer (a 41-byte file) that points to a commit SHA. Creating a branch is nearly instant and costs almost no disk space.
mcq.wrong_a: Branches do NOT copy files. They are just pointers — that's what makes Git branching so fast.
mcq.wrong_c: Git branches are not backups. They are simply named pointers into the commit graph.

mcq.q: What is HEAD in Git?
opts: A) The first commit ever made in the repository
B) A special pointer that tracks which branch or commit you currently have checked out
C) The remote server address stored in .git/config
mcq.explain: HEAD is a symbolic reference to the currently checked-out branch (or commit in detached HEAD state). When you commit, the branch HEAD points to advances automatically.
mcq.wrong_a: The first commit is not called HEAD. HEAD always refers to your CURRENT position, not the beginning.
mcq.wrong_c: Remote server info is stored in .git/config under [remote], not in HEAD.

mcq.q: What is the modern command to create AND switch to a new branch called 'feature/login' in one step?
opts: A) git branch feature/login && git checkout feature/login
B) git switch -c feature/login
C) git new feature/login
mcq.explain: git switch -c <branch> (available from Git 2.23+) creates and switches to the new branch in a single command. The older equivalent is git checkout -b.
mcq.wrong_a: This works but is two commands. git switch -c does it in one modern command.
mcq.wrong_c: There is no 'git new' command.

mcq.q: You're on branch 'main'. You run 'git branch hotfix'. What happens?
opts: A) Git creates the 'hotfix' branch AND switches to it immediately
B) Git creates the 'hotfix' branch but you STAY on 'main'
C) Git merges 'main' into 'hotfix'
mcq.explain: git branch <name> ONLY creates the branch. It does not switch to it. Use git switch hotfix or git checkout hotfix afterward to move to it.
mcq.wrong_a: git branch alone never switches. Use git switch -c or git checkout -b to create AND switch in one step.
mcq.wrong_c: git branch does not merge anything. It only creates a new pointer.

cmd.scenario: You need to start working on a new login feature. Create a new branch called 'feature/login' and switch to it in one command.
cmd.task: Create and switch to a branch called 'feature/login':
cmd.hint: Use 'git switch -c' or 'git checkout -b' to create and switch at once.
cmd.output: Switched to a new branch 'feature/login'
cmd.why: git switch -c creates the branch and immediately moves HEAD to it, so your next commit lands on the new branch.

cmd.scenario: You want to see ALL branches in your local repository and which one you are currently on.
cmd.task: List all local branches and show the active one:
cmd.hint: Use 'git branch' without arguments to list branches. The active one has an asterisk.
cmd.output:
* feature/login
  main
  hotfix/navbar
cmd.why: git branch lists all local branches. The * marks the currently checked-out branch.

cmd.scenario: You finished working on 'feature/login' and need to switch back to 'main'.
cmd.task: Switch to the 'main' branch:
cmd.hint: Use 'git switch' or 'git checkout' followed by the branch name.
cmd.output:
Switched to branch 'main'
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
cmd.why: git switch main moves HEAD to point at the main branch and updates your working directory to match that branch's latest commit.

cmd.scenario: You merged 'feature/login' into 'main' and no longer need the branch. Delete it.
cmd.task: Delete the local branch 'feature/login':
cmd.hint: Use 'git branch -d' to safely delete a merged branch.
cmd.output: Deleted branch feature/login (was 7f2b91c).
cmd.why: git branch -d deletes a branch only if it has been fully merged into the current branch. Use -D to force-delete unmerged branches.

5.topic: Merging branches: git merge, fast-forward vs 3-way merge, merge conflicts

mcq.q: When does Git perform a 'fast-forward' merge instead of a '3-way' merge?
opts: A) When the target branch has new commits that the source branch doesn't have
B) When the base branch (e.g. main) has not diverged — no new commits since the feature branch was created
C) Fast-forward only happens on GitHub, not locally
mcq.explain: A fast-forward merge happens when the branch being merged into has NOT advanced since the feature branch was created. Git simply moves the pointer forward — no merge commit needed.
mcq.wrong_a: If the target branch has new commits of its own, Git cannot fast-forward — it must do a 3-way merge.
mcq.wrong_c: Fast-forward merges happen entirely locally. GitHub/GitLab can also perform them remotely.

mcq.q: What is a merge conflict?
opts: A) When two branches have different names
B) When Git cannot automatically decide which version of a file to keep because both branches changed the same lines
C) When the network connection drops during a git push
mcq.explain: A merge conflict occurs when both the source and target branches modified the same part of the same file. Git marks the conflict and asks YOU to decide which version to keep.
mcq.wrong_a: Branch names have no effect on whether a conflict occurs.
mcq.wrong_c: Merge conflicts are a local operation — network issues cause push/pull failures, not merge conflicts.

mcq.q: After resolving a merge conflict manually, what two commands complete the merge?
opts: A) git fix → git done
B) git add <resolved-file> → git commit
C) git merge --continue → git push
mcq.explain: After editing conflict markers out of the file, you stage the resolved file with git add, then git commit to finalize the merge commit.
mcq.wrong_a: There are no 'git fix' or 'git done' commands.
mcq.wrong_c: git merge --continue works for rebases, not standard merges. And git push comes later, not to complete the merge.

mcq.q: What markers does Git inject directly into a file when a merge conflict occurs?
opts: A) <<<<<<< HEAD, =======, and >>>>>>> branch_name
B) [CONFLICT_START] and [CONFLICT_END]
C) <!-- MERGE ERROR --> tags
mcq.explain: Git marks conflicting sections using <<<<<<< HEAD (your current branch), ======= (divider), and >>>>>>> branch_name (incoming branch).
mcq.wrong_b: Git uses angle bracket markers <<<<<<< and >>>>>>>, not square bracket tags.
mcq.wrong_c: Git uses standard diff markers <<<<<<< HEAD, not HTML comment tags.

mcq.q: What command can you run to abort a messy merge conflict and return to the state before running git merge?
opts: A) git merge --abort
B) git cancel merge
C) git reset --merge-undo
mcq.explain: git merge --abort cleanly stops the merge process and restores your working tree to the state before the merge command was executed.
mcq.wrong_b: There is no git cancel command in Git.
mcq.wrong_c: The standard flag to cancel an in-progress merge is --abort on the git merge command.

cmd.scenario: You finished feature/login and are on 'main'. You want to merge 'feature/login' into 'main'.
cmd.task: Merge the 'feature/login' branch into the current branch:
cmd.hint: Use 'git merge' followed by the branch name you want to merge in.
cmd.output:
Updating 3c1a44f..7f2b91c
Fast-forward
 auth.py | 48 ++++++++++++++++++
 1 file changed, 48 insertions(+)
cmd.why: git merge <branch> integrates the given branch's commits into your current branch.

cmd.scenario: You merged a feature branch but want the history to show an explicit merge commit even though fast-forward was possible.
cmd.task: Merge 'feature/nav' into the current branch with a forced merge commit (no fast-forward):
cmd.hint: Use 'git merge' with the '--no-ff' flag.
cmd.output:
Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
 nav.py | 10 ++++++++++
 1 file changed, 10 insertions(+)
cmd.why: git merge --no-ff always creates a merge commit, preserving the fact that a feature branch existed in the history graph.

cmd.scenario: You have a merge conflict in 'README.md'. After manually editing the file to resolve it, complete the merge.
cmd.task: Stage the resolved file and finalize the merge:
cmd.hint: Stage the file with git add, then commit to finalize.
cmd.output:
[main 9b2a11f] Merge branch 'feature/docs'
 1 file changed, 5 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)
cmd.why: After resolving conflict markers in a file, staging it tells Git the conflict is resolved. git commit then creates the merge commit.

cmd.scenario: A merge went wrong with too many conflicts and you want to cleanly cancel it and restore your branch.
cmd.task: Abort the currently conflicted merge operation:
cmd.hint: Use the --abort flag with git merge.
cmd.output: (Merge aborted, working tree restored to previous clean HEAD)
cmd.why: git merge --abort resets your index and working tree back to before git merge was run.

cmd.scenario: You want to check which branch you are on and see all commits reachable on your branch before merging.
cmd.task: View a graphical ASCII representation of commits across all branches:
cmd.hint: Use git log with the --graph and --oneline flags.
cmd.output:
* 7f2b91c (HEAD -> main) feat: login
| * a1b2c3d (feature) feat: signup
|/
* 3c1a44f initial commit
cmd.why: git log --graph draws an ASCII art tree of branching and merging history.

6.topic: Remote repositories: git remote, git push, git pull, GitHub

mcq.q: What does 'git push origin main' do?
opts: A) Downloads the latest commits from GitHub into your local main branch
B) Uploads your local 'main' branch commits to the remote named 'origin'
C) Creates a new remote server called 'origin'
mcq.explain: git push origin main sends (uploads) your committed local history on 'main' to the 'origin' remote, making it visible to collaborators.
mcq.wrong_a: Downloading from remote is git pull or git fetch, not git push.
mcq.wrong_c: git remote add creates a remote link. git push uses an EXISTING remote to upload.

mcq.q: What is the difference between 'git fetch' and 'git pull'?
opts: A) They are identical — just aliases for the same operation
B) git fetch downloads remote commits but doesn't merge them; git pull downloads AND merges automatically
C) git fetch only works for GitHub; git pull works for any remote
mcq.explain: git fetch safely downloads remote changes into tracking branches (origin/main) without touching your working files. git pull = git fetch + git merge in one step.
mcq.wrong_a: They are very different. git fetch is safe and non-destructive; git pull can trigger merges.
mcq.wrong_c: Both git fetch and git pull work with any remote, not just GitHub.

mcq.q: What is 'origin' in a typical Git remote setup?
opts: A) The first commit in the repository
B) The default alias/shortname for the remote repository URL you cloned from
C) The main branch name on the server
mcq.explain: 'origin' is simply the default name Git assigns to the remote repository when you clone. It's a shorthand alias for the full URL. You can rename it or add more remotes.
mcq.wrong_a: The first commit has no special name called 'origin'. It's just a regular commit.
mcq.wrong_c: 'main' or 'master' are common default branch names. 'origin' refers to the remote server, not a branch.

mcq.q: What does the -u flag do when running 'git push -u origin main'?
opts: A) It sets the upstream tracking reference so future pushes only require typing 'git push'
B) It unlocks the remote repository for writing
C) It unzips the files on GitHub automatically
mcq.explain: The -u (or --set-upstream) flag links your local branch to the remote branch, allowing subsequent git push and git pull commands to run without arguments.
mcq.wrong_b: -u does not unlock permissions; write access is controlled by SSH keys or tokens.
mcq.wrong_c: Git does not zip/unzip files on push; it transfers Git packfile objects.

mcq.q: How do you download a copy of an existing remote repository from GitHub to your computer for the first time?
opts: A) git clone <repository-url>
B) git download <repository-url>
C) git copy <repository-url>
mcq.explain: git clone copies an entire existing remote repository (all files, history, and branches) to a new local directory on your machine.
mcq.wrong_b: There is no git download command in Git.
mcq.wrong_c: The command to copy a repository is git clone, not git copy.

cmd.scenario: You started a new local project and want to link it to a GitHub repo at 'https://github.com/user/repo.git'.
cmd.task: Add a remote named 'origin' pointing to that URL:
cmd.hint: Use 'git remote add' followed by the name 'origin' and the URL.
cmd.output: (No output — remote added silently)
cmd.why: git remote add <name> <url> registers a remote repository alias. 'origin' is the conventional default name.

cmd.scenario: You started your workday and want to download teammates' newest commits from GitHub into your local branch.
cmd.task: Download and merge the latest remote commits into your active branch:
cmd.hint: Use the command that fetches AND merges in one step.
cmd.output:
Updating 3c1a44f..7f2b91c
Fast-forward
 2 files changed, 10 insertions(+)
cmd.why: git pull fetches from the remote and immediately merges the new commits into your current local branch.

cmd.scenario: You committed changes locally and want to upload them to GitHub so your team can see them.
cmd.task: Push your local 'main' branch commits to 'origin':
cmd.hint: Use 'git push' followed by the remote name and branch name.
cmd.output:

7.topic: Undoing changes: git restore, git reset (soft/mixed/hard), git revert

mcq.q: What does 'git reset --hard HEAD~1' do?
opts: A) Creates a new commit that undoes the last commit's changes
B) Moves the branch pointer back one commit AND deletes the changes from your working directory
C) Unstages all files but keeps the working directory changes
mcq.explain: git reset --hard moves the branch pointer AND resets the working directory and staging area to match. Changes from the erased commit are GONE unless you use git reflog to recover.
mcq.wrong_a: Creating a new undo commit is git revert, not git reset.
mcq.wrong_c: Keeping working directory changes while moving the branch pointer is git reset --mixed (the default).

mcq.q: Which command safely undoes a commit that has ALREADY been pushed to a shared remote?
opts: A) git reset --hard HEAD~1
B) git revert HEAD
C) git commit --undo
mcq.explain: git revert creates a NEW commit that inverses a previous commit's changes. This is safe for shared/public history because it doesn't rewrite existing commits.
mcq.wrong_a: git reset --hard rewrites history. Pushing after a reset requires force-push which breaks collaborators' histories.
mcq.wrong_c: There is no 'git commit --undo' command.

mcq.q: What does 'git restore myfile.py' do (without --staged)?
opts: A) Deletes myfile.py from the repository permanently
B) Discards unstaged changes in myfile.py, reverting it to the last committed version
C) Copies myfile.py to a backup folder
mcq.explain: git restore <file> discards working directory changes in that file, reverting it to the state of the last commit. This is irreversible — the uncommitted changes are lost.
mcq.wrong_a: git restore does not delete files from the repository.
mcq.wrong_c: Git does not create backup folders. git restore simply overwrites the working file with the committed version.

mcq.q: What is the main danger of running 'git reset --hard'?
opts: A) It permanently discards uncommitted changes in your working directory and staging area
B) It deletes your GitHub account repository
C) It requires you to reinstall Git
mcq.explain: git reset --hard wipes out all unstaged and staged changes in tracked files. If changes were never committed, they cannot be recovered.
mcq.wrong_b: git reset is a purely local command; it does not delete remote repositories.
mcq.wrong_c: It only affects repository commit state and files, never the Git installation.

mcq.q: If you want to unstage all currently staged files without altering any code in your working directory, what do you run?
opts: A) git restore --staged .
B) git clean -fd
C) git drop
mcq.explain: git restore --staged . (or git reset) clears the staging index while preserving all modifications in your working files.
mcq.wrong_b: git clean -fd deletes untracked files from disk, which would cause data loss!
mcq.wrong_c: There is no git drop command in Git.

cmd.scenario: You edited 'app.py' and made a mess. You want to throw away ALL your unstaged changes and restore it to the last committed version.
cmd.task: Discard unstaged changes in 'app.py':
cmd.hint: Use 'git restore' followed by the filename to discard working directory changes.
cmd.output: (app.py is restored to the last committed state — changes discarded)
cmd.why: git restore <file> overwrites the working copy with the version from the last commit, discarding unsaved changes.

cmd.scenario: You want to undo the last commit but KEEP the changes in your working directory (so you can re-stage them differently).
cmd.task: Undo the last commit, keeping files modified in the working directory:
cmd.hint: Use 'git reset' with '--mixed' (or no flag, since mixed is the default) and HEAD~1.
cmd.output:
Unstaged changes after reset:
M	auth.py
M	config.py
cmd.why: git reset --mixed HEAD~1 moves the branch pointer back but leaves your working directory changes intact, so you can re-stage and recommit differently.

cmd.scenario: You pushed a buggy commit to 'main'. You need to undo it safely without rewriting shared history.
cmd.task: Create a new commit that reverses the effect of the last commit:
cmd.hint: Use 'git revert' to create an inverse commit of HEAD.
cmd.output:
[main 8c3d11a] Revert "fix: broken auth logic"
 1 file changed, 5 deletions(-)
cmd.why: git revert HEAD creates a new commit that is the exact inverse of HEAD's changes. Safe for shared history since it does not rewrite existing commits.

cmd.scenario: You staged several files with 'git add .' by mistake, but want to unstage all of them while keeping your code intact.

cmd.hint: Use git clean with the -f (force) and -d (directory) flags.
cmd.output:
Removing temp_notes.txt
Removing build_cache/
cmd.why: git clean -fd permanently deletes untracked files and directories to keep the workspace spotless.

8.topic: Stashing work: git stash, git stash pop, git stash list, git stash drop

mcq.q: When should you use 'git stash'?
opts: A) When you want to permanently delete uncommitted changes
B) When you need to switch branches but have uncommitted work you don't want to commit yet
C) When you want to push changes to GitHub without committing
mcq.explain: git stash temporarily saves your uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged) onto a stack, giving you a clean working directory to switch contexts, then restores them later.
mcq.wrong_a: git stash saves changes — it does NOT delete them. Use git restore or git reset for discarding.
mcq.wrong_c: You cannot push uncommitted changes to GitHub. git stash is purely a local operation.

mcq.q: What does 'git stash pop' do?
opts: A) Deletes the most recent stash permanently
B) Applies the most recent stash back to the working directory AND removes it from the stash list
C) Shows the contents of the most recent stash without applying it
mcq.explain: git stash pop applies the top stash entry to your working directory and removes it from the stash stack — like popping from a stack data structure.
mcq.wrong_a: git stash drop permanently deletes a stash. git stash pop restores AND removes.
mcq.wrong_c: git stash show displays stash contents without applying. git stash pop both applies and removes.

mcq.q: How do you apply a stash WITHOUT removing it from the stash list?
opts: A) git stash pop
B) git stash keep
C) git stash apply
mcq.explain: git stash apply applies a stash entry to your working directory but keeps it in the stash list. Useful when you want to apply the same stash to multiple branches.
mcq.wrong_a: git stash pop applies AND removes from the list.
mcq.wrong_b: There is no 'git stash keep' command.

mcq.q: What does 'git stash drop' do?
opts: A) It permanently deletes a specific stash entry without applying it
B) It applies a stash to your working directory and commits it
C) It pauses your active terminal session
mcq.explain: git stash drop removes a specific stash from your stash stack permanently without restoring its changes.
mcq.wrong_b: Applying a stash is done via git stash apply or git stash pop, not drop.
mcq.wrong_c: git stash only manipulates Git storage, not terminal processes.

mcq.q: By default, does 'git stash' save untracked (newly created) files?
opts: A) No, you must pass the -u (or --include-untracked) flag to stash untracked files
B) Yes, git stash always stashes everything including untracked and ignored files
C) Untracked files can never be stashed under any circumstances
mcq.explain: By default git stash only stashes tracked modified files. To stash newly created untracked files, pass '-u' or '--include-untracked'.
mcq.wrong_b: Standard git stash ignores untracked files unless -u is explicitly specified.
mcq.wrong_c: Untracked files CAN be stashed using the -u / --include-untracked flag.

cmd.scenario: You're in the middle of editing 'feature.py' but your boss asks you to urgently fix a bug on 'main'. Save your work without committing.
cmd.task: Stash your current uncommitted changes with the description 'WIP: feature work':
cmd.hint: Use 'git stash push -m' or 'git stash save' with a descriptive message.
cmd.output: Saved working directory and index state On feature: WIP: feature work
cmd.why: git stash push -m saves all uncommitted changes (staged + unstaged) onto the stash stack with a readable label.

cmd.scenario: You fixed the urgent bug and want to retrieve your stashed feature work.
cmd.task: Apply the most recent stash and remove it from the stash list:
cmd.hint: Use 'git stash pop' to restore the latest stash entry.
cmd.output:
On branch feature
Changes not staged for commit:
	modified:   feature.py
Dropped refs/stash@{0}
cmd.why: git stash pop restores your stashed work to the working directory and removes it from the stash stack.

cmd.scenario: You have multiple stashes saved and want to see all of them before choosing which to restore.
cmd.task: List all saved stash entries:
cmd.hint: Use 'git stash' followed by 'list' to see all stash entries.
cmd.output:
stash@{0}: On feature: WIP: feature work
stash@{1}: On main: hotfix temp changes
stash@{2}: WIP on docs: README updates
cmd.why: git stash list shows all stash entries with their index (stash@{0} is most recent), branch name, and message.

cmd.scenario: You created a new file 'api.py' (untracked) and modified 'app.py'. You want to stash BOTH files including the untracked file.
cmd.task: Stash all changes including untracked files:
cmd.hint: Use git stash with the -u flag for untracked files.
cmd.output:
Saved working directory and index state WIP on main: 7f2b91c
(Untracked files included in stash)
cmd.why: git stash -u captures both modified tracked files and newly created untracked files onto the stash.

cmd.scenario: You want to completely clear and delete ALL saved stashes in your repository.
cmd.task: Delete all saved stashes on the stash list:
cmd.hint: Use the command: git stash clear
cmd.output: (All stash entries cleared from refs/stash)
cmd.why: git stash clear removes all stashed states from the repository stack.

9.topic: Rebasing: git rebase, interactive rebase, squashing commits

mcq.q: What is the key difference between 'git merge' and 'git rebase'?
opts: A) git merge is faster than git rebase for large repos
B) git rebase rewrites commit history to create a linear sequence; git merge preserves the branch structure with a merge commit
C) git rebase can only be done on GitHub, not locally
mcq.explain: git rebase moves your branch's commits to start from the tip of another branch, rewriting their SHAs to create a clean linear history. git merge keeps the original branch topology.
mcq.wrong_a: Speed is not the defining difference — both are fast locally.
mcq.wrong_c: git rebase is a local Git command. It can be performed entirely offline.

mcq.q: What does 'git rebase -i HEAD~3' allow you to do?
opts: A) Rebases the last 3 commits onto a remote branch
B) Opens an interactive editor to reorder, squash, edit, or drop the last 3 commits
C) Reverts the last 3 commits and creates 3 undo commits
mcq.explain: git rebase -i (interactive) opens your editor with a list of the specified commits. You can squash them together, reword messages, reorder them, or drop unwanted ones.
mcq.wrong_a: git rebase -i HEAD~3 operates on LOCAL commits only. No remote is involved.
mcq.wrong_c: git revert creates undo commits. git rebase -i rewrites existing commits.

mcq.q: What does 'squashing' commits mean in an interactive rebase?
opts: A) Compressing commit files into a zip archive
B) Combining multiple commits into a single unified commit
C) Force-pushing commits to overwrite the remote
mcq.explain: Squashing (using 's' or 'squash' in the interactive rebase editor) folds a commit into the one above it, combining their changes into one clean commit. Great for cleaning up WIP history.
mcq.wrong_a: Git does not create zip archives during rebase.
mcq.wrong_c: Force-push is a separate operation (git push --force) used after rewriting history, not part of squashing itself.

mcq.q: What is the Golden Rule of Rebasing?
opts: A) Never rebase commits that exist outside your local repository and have been pushed to a public/shared branch
B) Always rebase before every commit
C) Rebasing should only be done on Friday afternoons
mcq.explain: Rebasing rewrites commit hashes. If other developers have based their work on the original commits, rewriting shared history creates duplicate commits and merge nightmares.
mcq.wrong_b: You do not need to rebase before every commit; only when integrating upstream changes cleanly.
mcq.wrong_c: Never rewrite shared history on any day of the week!

mcq.q: In an interactive rebase (git rebase -i), which command rewrites the commit message while keeping the changes intact?
opts: A) reword (or r)
B) fixup (or f)
C) drop (or d)
mcq.explain: The 'reword' command pauses during interactive rebase and lets you edit the commit log message without altering the file diffs.
mcq.wrong_b: fixup discards the commit message and merges diffs into the parent commit.
mcq.wrong_c: drop completely deletes the commit.

cmd.why: git rebase -i HEAD~4 opens the interactive rebase editor for the last 4 commits, letting you squash, reorder, or drop them.

cmd.scenario: During a rebase, you ran into a merge conflict. After resolving the conflict and staging the files, you want to continue the rebase.
cmd.task: Continue the in-progress rebase after resolving conflicts:
cmd.hint: Use git rebase with the --continue flag.
cmd.output:
Applying: feat: add billing module
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature.
cmd.why: git rebase --continue resumes applying remaining commits after a conflict is resolved.

cmd.scenario: A rebase went horribly wrong and you want to cancel it completely and return to your original branch state.
cmd.task: Abort the currently in-progress rebase:
cmd.hint: Use git rebase with the --abort flag.
cmd.output: (Rebase aborted, HEAD returned to original commit)

cmd.scenario: You want to check the status of an ongoing rebase to see which commit is currently paused with conflicts.

10.topic: Advanced Git: git cherry-pick, git bisect, git reflog, git tag

mcq.q: What does 'git cherry-pick <commit-sha>' do?
opts: A) Deletes the specified commit from history
B) Applies the changes from a specific commit onto your current branch as a new commit
C) Reverts the specified commit and its parent
mcq.explain: git cherry-pick copies a specific commit's changes and applies them as a new commit on the current branch. Useful for pulling a hotfix from one branch into another without merging everything.
mcq.wrong_a: To delete a commit, you use git reset or git rebase -i with 'drop'. git cherry-pick only copies.
mcq.wrong_c: git revert undoes a commit. git cherry-pick applies one.

mcq.q: What is 'git reflog' used for?
opts: A) Viewing the log of commits on a remote branch
B) Recovering commits or branches that were lost due to a hard reset or accidental deletion
C) Listing all refs (branches and tags) alphabetically
mcq.explain: git reflog records every movement of HEAD in your local repository — including resets, checkouts, and rebases. It's your safety net for recovering 'lost' commits after destructive operations.
mcq.wrong_a: git log --remotes or git log origin/main shows remote commits. git reflog is local HEAD movements.
mcq.wrong_c: git show-ref or git branch -a lists refs. git reflog is a time-stamped history of HEAD movements.

mcq.q: What is the purpose of 'git bisect'?
opts: A) To split a commit into two separate commits
B) To perform a binary search through commit history to find which commit introduced a bug
C) To split a repository into two separate repos
mcq.explain: git bisect performs a binary search: you mark one commit as 'good' and one as 'bad', then Git checks out the midpoint commit for you to test. It halves the search space with each step.
mcq.wrong_a: Splitting a commit is done with git reset + multiple commits or git rebase -i.
mcq.wrong_c: Splitting a repository is a separate operation not done with git bisect.

mcq.q: What is a lightweight tag in Git compared to an annotated tag?
opts: A) A lightweight tag is just a pointer to a commit (like a bookmark); an annotated tag is a full Git object with author, date, and message
B) A lightweight tag only works for text files
C) A lightweight tag expires after 30 days
mcq.explain: Lightweight tags (git tag v1.0) are simply bookmarks pointing to a commit hash. Annotated tags (git tag -a v1.0 -m 'msg') store checksum, tagger details, date, and a GPG signature if configured.
mcq.wrong_b: Tags point to commits, never individual files.
mcq.wrong_c: Git tags never expire; they are permanent references until explicitly deleted.

mcq.q: When running 'git bisect', what command tells Git that the currently checked out commit is working properly (does NOT contain the bug)?
opts: A) git bisect good
B) git bisect clean
C) git bisect pass
mcq.explain: git bisect good marks the current commit as bug-free, prompting Git to bisect toward the bad commit.
mcq.wrong_b: The keywords for bisect are 'good' and 'bad' (or terms like old/new), not clean.
mcq.wrong_c: The valid command is 'git bisect good'.

[main 9f3c21a] fix: resolve null pointer in auth
 Date: Mon Nov 10 2026
 1 file changed, 3 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)
cmd.why: git cherry-pick <sha> copies just that commit's diff and applies it as a new commit on your current branch.

cmd.scenario: You accidentally did a hard reset and lost commits. You want to find the SHA of the lost commit to recover it.
cmd.task: Show the full log of recent HEAD movements to find the lost commit SHA:
cmd.hint: Use 'git reflog' to see every position HEAD has been at.
cmd.output:
7f2b91c HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~2
a1b2c3d HEAD@{1}: commit: feat: add payment gateway
3c1a44f HEAD@{2}: commit: fix: cart total calculation
cmd.why: git reflog records every movement of HEAD locally. Even after hard resets, the original commit SHAs are listed here so you can recover them with git reset or git checkout.

cmd.scenario: You released version 1.0.0 and want to mark that commit permanently with a tag.
cmd.task: Create an annotated tag 'v1.0.0' on the current commit with the message 'First stable release':
cmd.hint: Use 'git tag -a' for an annotated tag with '-m' for the message.
cmd.output: (Tag v1.0.0 created pointing to current commit)

cmd.scenario: You have a bug that appeared sometime in the last 100 commits. You want Git to help you find it automatically.

cmd.why: git bisect start initializes the binary search. git bisect bad marks the current commit as one that exhibits the bug.

cmd.scenario: You finished finding a bug with git bisect and want to end the session and return to your original branch.

cmd.hint: Use the command: git bisect reset
cmd.output:
Previous HEAD position was a1b2c3d
Switched to branch 'main'
cmd.why: git bisect reset cleans up the bisect state and returns your working tree and HEAD back to where you started.
